results.term_definition: From the perspective of an observer on Earth, when two astronomical objects appear to be in close proximity in the sky they are said to be in conjunction. The conjunction does not need to be actually visible – for instance, the Moon and the Sun are approximately lined up whenever there is a new Moon, but we cannot see the Moon under those conditions, unless there is a solar eclipse. In that case, and whenever a conjunction is so close that one object appears to cover the other, astronomers would describe it as a transit or eclipse.
